title: 2 Kings 15:17–31
context: Menahem reigns ten years and pays a heavy tribute to Pul of Assyria to secure his throne. His son Pekahiah reigns two years before his captain Pekah kills him. During Pekah's reign Tiglath-pileser of Assyria takes much of the north, including Galilee and Naphtali, and deports its people. Hoshea then kills Pekah and takes the throne. Pul is often identified with Tiglath-pileser, though that identification is discussed. Pekah's twenty-year figure in verse 27 raises chronological questions that interpreters explain in more than one way, including overlapping or rival reigns. The passage shows Israel's rapid decline under Assyrian pressure.

verses.text: In the thirty ninth year of Azariah king of Judah, Menahem the son of Gadi began to reign over Israel for ten years in Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes: Menahem reigns ten years in Samaria. Arminian readers note that, unlike his two predecessors, he holds power long enough to have real opportunity to lead the nation differently.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Menahem's ten years seem like stability compared with the coups around them. Yet the next verses show that his security rests on violence and foreign money, not on God.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight. He didn’t depart all his days from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, with which he made Israel to sin.
verses.arminianNotes: He does evil and does not depart "all his days" from Jeroboam's sins. Arminian readers note the emphasis on the whole span of his reign; ten years passed without any turning back to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the added phrase "all his days." The length of a reign does not change its direction when the heart remains fixed on the sins of Jeroboam.

verses.text: Pul the king of Assyria came against the land, and Menahem gave Pul one thousand talents of silver, that his hand might be with him to confirm the kingdom in his hand.
verses.arminianNotes: Pul king of Assyria comes, and Menahem pays a thousand talents of silver to secure his kingdom. Arminian readers see a king choosing to trust Assyria's power rather than God's protection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 1 Chronicles 5:26 says God "stirred up the spirit of Pul" and Tiglath-pileser; many identify Pul with Tiglath-pileser. Assyria's advance is under God's hand.

verses.text: Menahem exacted the money from Israel, even from all the mighty men of wealth, from each man fifty shekels of silver, to give to the king of Assyria. So the king of Assyria turned back, and didn’t stay there in the land.
verses.arminianNotes: Menahem taxes the wealthy men of Israel fifty shekels each to pay Assyria. Arminian readers note the burden passed to the people, the cost of a king's decision to buy security rather than seek God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Assyrian king turns back, but only for a price. Psalm 146:3 warns, "Don’t put your trust in princes," and Israel's purchased relief proves temporary.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Menahem, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Menahem's acts are in the chronicles of the kings of Israel. Arminian readers note that his reign is remembered chiefly for brutality and tribute, the choices that marked his leadership.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the standard formula closes Menahem's reign. The narrative has given what matters: his evil, his violence, and his dependence on Assyria.

verses.text: Menahem slept with his fathers, and Pekahiah his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Menahem dies and Pekahiah succeeds him. Arminian readers note that Menahem is one of the few kings of this period to die naturally and pass the throne to a son.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the brief moment of dynastic succession. In a kingdom of coups, an orderly transfer is noteworthy, but it will not last beyond two years.

verses.text: In the fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah, Pekahiah the son of Menahem began to reign over Israel in Samaria for two years.
verses.arminianNotes: Pekahiah reigns two years in Samaria. Arminian readers note that the son inherits not only his father's throne but also his father's precarious position under Assyria.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Pekahiah's reign is dated by the fiftieth year of Azariah. Judah's long reign contrasts sharply with the instability of Israel's throne.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight. He didn’t depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, with which he made Israel to sin.
verses.arminianNotes: He does evil and continues Jeroboam's sins. Arminian readers note that he, too, chooses the established path of false worship rather than turning the nation back to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the same verdict is repeated almost word for word. Each generation inherits and continues the sin, and none breaks the pattern.

verses.text: Pekah the son of Remaliah, his captain, conspired against him and attacked him in Samaria, in the fortress of the king’s house, with Argob and Arieh; and with him were fifty men of the Gileadites. He killed him, and reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: His captain Pekah, with fifty Gileadites, kills him in the palace fortress. Arminian readers see betrayal by a trusted officer, another free and violent choice in Israel's descent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the coup takes place inside the king's own fortress. No stronghold can protect a throne that God has given up to the consequences of its sin.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Pekahiah, and all that he did, behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Pekahiah's acts are recorded elsewhere. Arminian readers note that two years leave a brief record, ended by the treachery of one of his own officers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the closing formula for yet another short reign. The repetition of the pattern itself becomes part of the narrator's message about Israel's decline.

verses.text: In the fifty-second year of Azariah king of Judah, Pekah the son of Remaliah began to reign over Israel in Samaria for twenty years.
verses.arminianNotes: Pekah reigns over Israel in Samaria for twenty years. Arminian readers note that the length of his reign raises chronological questions that interpreters discuss, but the narrative focus remains on his conduct.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that many interpreters explain the twenty years through overlapping or rival reigns; the text itself simply gives the figure, and the moral verdict is the narrator's main concern.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight. He didn’t depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, with which he made Israel to sin.
verses.arminianNotes: He does evil and continues Jeroboam's sins. Arminian readers note that even a long reign yields no reform, as Pekah chooses the same path as every king before him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the unbroken refrain. Israel's kings change by violence, but the nation's worship never changes, and the end draws closer.

verses.text: In the days of Pekah king of Israel, Tiglath Pileser king of Assyria came and took Ijon, Abel Beth Maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali; and he carried them captive to Assyria.
verses.arminianNotes: Tiglath-pileser takes much of the north, including Galilee and Naphtali, and deports the people. Arminian readers see the warnings of the prophets beginning to come true as Israel experiences the first wave of exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this partial deportation anticipates the full exile in 2 Kings 17:6. God's covenant warnings are fulfilled in stages, giving time for repentance that does not come.

verses.text: Hoshea the son of Elah made a conspiracy against Pekah the son of Remaliah, attacked him, killed him, and reigned in his place, in the twentieth year of Jotham the son of Uzziah.
verses.arminianNotes: Hoshea conspires against Pekah, kills him, and reigns. Arminian readers note that the cycle of violence continues to the last king of Israel, each ruler overthrown by another.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Hoshea will be Israel's final king (2 Kings 17:6). The coup that brings him to power marks the last turn before the end of the northern kingdom.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Pekah, and all that he did, behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Pekah's acts are in the chronicles of the kings of Israel. Arminian readers note that Pekah's reign is remembered for decline and territorial loss under Assyria.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the closing formula. As Pekah's reign ends, the narrative turns back to Judah, where his alliance with Syria will soon threaten Ahaz.
